text.text: A ten-minute tour of the fleet in this workspace. Share it with the dispatcher, the fleet maintenance lead, the owner and the office.
: every load with customer, lane, truck, driver, windows, rate, loaded and empty miles, rate per mile, detention, delivery receipt and billing.
: each tractor and trailer with status, miles, service and inspection dates, revenue booked and delivered loads not yet paid.
: each driver's day from the electronic log, with hours left in the 70-hour cycle.
: scheduled service, inspections and repairs, with cost and mileage.
: licenses, medical cards, testing and training, with expiry dates.
Morning: loads picking up today confirmed; drivers' hours checked.
Through the day: check-ins at pickup and delivery; problems called in.
Afternoon: tomorrow's loads assigned; delivered loads invoiced.
Evening: hours of service entered from the logs.
Every morning: loads today, drivers' hours, trucks in the shop
Every week: maintenance due in 14 days, unpaid invoices over 30 days
Every month: rate per mile by customer, documents expiring
Every quarter: maintenance cost per truck, customer review
The dispatcher books and assigns loads and watches hours. The maintenance lead owns trucks and service. The office invoices and chases payment. The owner sets rates and reads the Dashboard.

No load is worth a tired driver or an unsafe truck. Any driver can refuse a load they cannot run legally or safely, and dispatch backs them every time. Roadside inspections, warnings and accidents are recorded the same day and reviewed with the driver.

Rename units, lanes and customers, set your own cost per mile in the dispatch routine, and delete the sample rows once your own are in. Edit any cell in place; rates per mile and hours left update by themselves.

A customer offers Tulsa to Denver at $3,600 for 680 loaded miles, about $5.29 a mile, with 85 empty miles to the pickup. The total-mile rate is $4.71, above cost. Natasha has 18 hours left in her cycle after tomorrow, so the dispatcher books the load for her, and plans a return load before she leaves Denver.

A truck that breaks down on the road costs a tow, a missed delivery and a customer's trust. Preventive maintenance on a schedule is far cheaper than repairs, and it keeps you ready for a roadside inspection.
. Typical intervals for a long-haul tractor:
Oil and filter: every 15,000 to 25,000 miles, by the engine maker's guide.
Brake check: at every service; adjust and replace pads by measurement, not by calendar.
Tires: tread depth and pressure every week; steer tires replaced before 4/32 of an inch.
Annual inspection: every 12 months, with the sticker and report in the truck file.
Trailers: lights, brakes, tires and doors at every service.

Drivers inspect before and after every trip: lights, tires, brakes, coupling, fluid leaks. Anything wrong is written on the inspection report. The maintenance lead signs off each defect as fixed or not affecting safety before the truck goes out.
